Sources & data notes

Source data: the three federal land-managing agencies' own published Class I area boundary shapefiles — USFWS fwsClassI (final, 21 areas), NPS npsClassI (dated 2007-11-19, 48 areas), and USFS USFSC1 (final, NAD83 geographic, 88 areas). These are boundary files for the mandatory federal Class I areas designated under Clean Air Act §162(a): national parks >6,000 acres, national wilderness areas >5,000 acres, and national memorial parks >5,000 acres that existed as of August 7, 1977. 21 + 48 + 88 = 157 areas in this build; the commonly cited count is 156, and this build has not reconciled that one-area difference against an EPA reference list — treat the area list here as sourced directly from the three agencies' own shapefiles, not cross-checked against EPA's count.

Corrections applied to the source attribute data (not silent — listed in full here):

  • NPS chir (Chiricahua) carries two sub-polygons under one ID: one tagged "Not Studied" and one tagged "Designated Wilderness." Only the Designated Wilderness polygon is an actual Class I boundary; the Not Studied polygon is excluded from this area's geometry and area total.
  • NPS badl (Badlands): the source State attribute reads "ND". Badlands National Park, and its Sage Creek Wilderness unit shown here, are entirely in South Dakota. Displayed as SD.
  • Ten area groups (of 157) carry more than one distinct Name across their sub-polygons — multi-unit refuges/parks such as Bosque del Apache (three units), Point Reyes/Phillip Burton Wilderness (three tracts), Badlands (two tracts), Denali ("NP" vs "NP and Wilderness"), and similar. Each was given one hand-chosen canonical name rather than a mechanical text merge; the source Name variants are not otherwise altered.
  • "Virgin Island NP" (source typo, missing the "s") is displayed as Virgin Islands National Park. "Great Sand Dunes Wilderness-nps" has the "-nps" tag stripped from the display name.

Geometry: polygons are simplified (Douglas-Peucker, ~50 m tolerance in a locally latitude-corrected projection) from the source boundaries, which were digitized at scales from 1:24,000 to 1:2,000,000 depending on agency and area. At the 300 km scale this tool is built for, 50 m of boundary generalization is not meaningful. Areas (mi²) are computed from the merged geometry (spherical area), not copied from the shapefiles' own per-polygon area attributes, so figures are internally consistent across all three sources.

Distance: "Dist km"/"Dist mi" is the great-circle distance from the draggable reference point to the nearest point on the area's boundary (edge-by-edge spherical cross-track distance), not distance to a centroid. This matches how distance is used in a Q/D (significant impact) screening calculation under 40 CFR 51 Appendix W/Y. If the reference point falls inside an area's boundary, distance is reported as 0. The map centroid (used only to place the map label) is a separate, less precise point and is not what the table sorts or filters on.

PSD Class I increments shown above are the fixed values in 40 CFR 51.166(c) / 52.21(c) — they do not vary by area, area type, or managing agency, so they are shown once rather than repeated identically on all 157 rows. Confirm current values against the regulation text before using them in a permit submission; increments have changed by rulemaking before (most recently the 2010 PM2.5 increments) and could again.

What this tool does not do: it does not determine which Class I areas are subject to AQRV (visibility, deposition) review for a given source, does not run or replace a CALPUFF/CALMET or plume visibility analysis, and does not know about state-only Class I designations (none exist federally beyond these 157, but some states/tribes have their own analogous programs). Reference-point search and radius filtering are for scoping which areas merit a closer look, not a substitute for the modeling itself.
